description:
MEDIUM. Flat vector fills, no strokes, no texture, no gradient, no noise. Every token is a stack of translucent regular shapes -- circles, squares, hexagons, diamonds, and 10-to-12-point star polygons -- laid concentrically on a common centre over a near-black blue-grey ground. The whole collection is drawn in ONE narrow hue family: an ochre/amber/mustard yellow at a low alpha. Because the fills are translucent and stacked, the alpha multiplies where they pile up, so the centre of each token is a heavy flat cocoa-brown and the outer petals that overlap least are the brightest gold. That accumulation IS the entire tonal system; there is no second colour, no light source, no line work.

WHAT IT IS A PICTURE OF. Nothing representational, but it reads consistently as an emblem: a rosette, a seal, a wax stamp, a sunburst medallion, a mandala. A few seeds tip toward diagram instead -- 9369 is a large disc with a chain of three progressively smaller discs budding off its right flank, which reads as a planet with moons, or a cell dividing, or a ball-and-socket. 9727 and 9906 read as a core with limbs.

WHAT THE TWELVE SHARE. One centred cluster per frame, near-radial symmetry, the same shape vocabulary, the same single hue, the same ground, the same concentric alpha-stacking logic, and the same figure-in-the-middle placement. They are unmistakably one family.

HOW THEY DIFFER. Chiefly by base silhouette and by whether the core sprouts satellites. Round: 9369. Square/rectilinear: 9190, 10801, 10622. Hexagonal: 10085. Diamond: 10443. Star/rosette: 9011, 10980, 10264, 9548. Satellite chains of shrinking shapes radiate at angles in 9548 (three arms), 9727 (three long arms, the most sprawling frame in the set), 9906 (two arms), 9369 (one chain of three), 10980 (one arm). Density ranges from very sparse -- 10443 is one small brown diamond with two ochre wedges and a great deal of empty ground -- to dense and bright, 10264 being a burst of many overlapping gold polygons that is the loudest tile on the sheet. 10085 is the quietest: a dull brown hexagon over a dull brown square, so low in contrast it is barely separable from the ground.

ACROSS THE THREE STATES. The change is large, monotone in one direction, and legible without comparison. Neutral is the mid setting. STRESS strips the work: the satellite appendages disappear entirely, the cluster contracts toward its centre, layer count drops, and the colour desaturates to a flat dull brown -- 9548 loses all three of its arms and becomes a bare 12-point star; 9369 collapses from a large disc to a small one and its moon-chain shrinks to a single dot; 9190 shrinks inside its own square. RECOVERY does the opposite and overshoots neutral: everything grows past the neutral footprint, gains layers, the appendages return larger and more numerous (9548 recovery has more arms than 9548 neutral), and the hue saturates to a bright, almost lemon gold. Read as a row, it is contraction/desaturation then expansion/saturation.

WHAT SURVIVES AT 120px. The state axis survives completely -- the stress row is instantly dimmer, smaller and simpler and the recovery row instantly brighter and larger, with no need to compare tiles. Seed identity survives only partly. The silhouette families (round, square, diamond, armed, burst) are still readable, and 9369, 10443 and 10264 stand clearly apart from the rest. But 9011, 10622 and 10980 are close relatives at browse size -- brown mass with a gold fringe -- and in the STRESS row 9011 and 9548 become effectively the same image, a dull brown twelve-point star with nothing to tell them apart. 10085 at 120px is close to an undifferentiated dark rectangle.

ARTIFACTS I NOTICE. Shapes run off the frame in several tiles: 10801's large square is cut by the left and bottom edges and reads as mis-sized rather than cropped; 10264's gold polygons are clipped at the right and bottom; 10980 is clipped top and right; 9727's upper-left arm reaches the left edge. Separately, the interiors are inert -- in most tokens the central two-thirds is one large flat brown mass with almost no incident, and all the drawing happens in the fringe, so the eye has nothing to do once it has read the outline.
